title: Come with me if you want a BIG BACK (4 steps MASSterplan)
summary: A four-step back masterplan that builds from three lifts a week (hinge, vertical pull, horizontal pull) to up to seven exercises plus rotating variations. Volume is added only when progress needs it, sets are capped at each step, and back work is spread through the week with no more than three back exercises in one session.
claims: The masterplans are general guidelines for one body part to integrate into your existing program, not full programs
Start at the step that matches your training level; complete novices begin at step 1
Step 1: pick one hip hinge, one vertical pull and one horizontal pull, each on a different day of the week
Any hip hinge works (deadlift, RDL, good morning, even hyperextension); there is no need to force the deadlift
Pull-ups are preferable as the vertical pull, but a lat pulldown is fine if you cannot do them yet; aim to get to pull-ups for later weighted work
Choose a horizontal pull that does not load the legs and lower back (dumbbell or cable row); a heavy barbell row counts as a hip hinge
If you train back only twice a week, pair the hinge with one pull and never do the vertical and horizontal pull on the same day in step 1
Training more days than three in step 1 does not mean adding back sets, just a day without back
Deadlifts: 3x3 or 3x5 is the volume ceiling for beginners, and 1x3 or 1x5 can work well because deadlifts are very fatiguing
RDLs, good mornings or hyperextensions: 2-4 sets of 6-10 or 8-12; two hard sets of heavy RDLs can be enough for the posterior chain
Intensity drives growth; extra volume should be a last resort for continued growth
Bodyweight pull-ups: as many reps as possible to failure for 3-4 sets, once a week
Lat pulldown 3-4 sets of 8-12; rows (dumbbell, seal, cable) 6-10 or 8-12, 10-15 also possible
Barbell rows should be programmed as the day's hinge, opening the session, for 6-10 reps; going lower degrades form
Pick exercises you enjoy within each movement pattern because enjoyment aids adherence
Beginners can grow with almost no work; enjoy it and do not add more volume than needed
Move to step 2 when your back feels it can take more after the session
Step 2: add one more hip hinge and one more pull (vertical or horizontal) as additions, not rotations
For carryover pick a 'soft' variation close to the main lift (pull-up -> lat pulldown); bodybuilders can also pick 'hard' variations for variety since specificity matters less
Use different rep ranges on second exercises of the same pattern (e.g. deadlift 3x3, good morning 3x6-10; dumbbell row 6-10, cable row 8-12)
Place the second hinge as far as possible from the first; if days run out, put it on the same day as the first exercise to protect recovery
Never do more than two back exercises in one session in step 2, and never two from the same family
Introduce new exercises with 1-2 sets and cut existing ones to 2 sets, then add a set per week or two up to 4 sets each
Adding sets over time is itself a form of progressive overload
Any back exercise will grow the back; details only shift emphasis between lats and traps
Once you hit 10 clean bodyweight pull-ups, start weighted pull-ups for 3-4 sets of 3-5 clean reps with the same grip and technique
A second vertical pull alongside weighted pull-ups can be bodyweight chest-to-bar pull-ups, a new grip, or lat pulldowns 8-12 to rest tendons
Pull-ups are S-tier for the upper back, especially lats
Step 1 caps at about 12 weekly back sets and step 2 at 20; only go higher when you can recover and progress at the current cap
Spend at least 6 months to a year on each step
The back tolerates more volume than arms, for which 20 weekly sets would be too much
Train back exercises to failure except hip hinges (leave a rep in reserve) and possibly pull-ups if you cannot grind them safely
Step 3: add one more pull or shrug; any new hinge comes only as a weekly alternating variation (e.g. week A deadlift 3x3, week B RDL 3x8-12)
Add pullovers in step 3, ideally dumbbell or machine (not cable); they stretch the lats differently from any pull-up
Leave at least 48 hours between back sessions even if it means doing two back exercises the same day; prioritize recovery over per-exercise performance
Hitting back six days a week with one exercise each is a bad idea because overlapping pulls hurt next-day performance
Step 3 caps at 12-24 weekly sets; many lifters never need more and can keep growing there by fluctuating volume
Only increase volume when necessary for progression
Step 4: add one exercise and two variations for 14-28 weekly sets; this range covers 99.9% of lifters' needs
HIT's fixed minimal-set rule keeps those who need more small, but doing as many sets as possible is also wrong; do as little as needed for as much growth as possible
Rotating variations helps progression, but if lifts regress from too little frequency, cut back the variations
Never train back every day and never do more than three back exercises in one session; after two or three exercises the work is mostly wasted
With seven back exercises: split 2-3-2 over three days or 2-1-2-2 style over four
Hypertrophy programming should not be complicated; theory without application is worthless
